summary: Looks at case studies of Internet protocols to ask which factors contribute to or hinder a protocol's success. The aim is to offer guidance for future protocol design work. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5218 uses protocol case studies to examine why some designs gain use and others do not. It concludes that solving a real problem and allowing gradual deployment matter strongly at first, while extensibility, scalability, and security matter as use expands.

questions: how should i design a protocol to succeed
what matters more technical quality or easy deployment
what factors make an internet protocol successful
subtitle: A case-study-based look at factors that help Internet protocols succeed or fail.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols have had different outcomes, and protocol designers need to understand which factors support adoption and wider use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares successful and unsuccessful protocol case studies and separates factors for initial success from factors for success beyond the original design.
tldr.outcome: The report finds that meeting a real need and incremental deployment are especially important at first. Extensibility, scalability, and security affect whether a protocol can grow further.

today: RFC 5218 is Informational and was published in July 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Meanings of Protocol Success
sections.content:
The RFC calls a protocol successful when it meets its original goals and is widely deployed. A protocol is wildly successful when it is used at much larger scale or for purposes beyond its original design.

Wild success can expose design limits. A protocol may face performance problems, harmful side effects, or attacks when people use it in ways its designers did not anticipate. The RFC therefore treats initial adoption and later growth as separate questions.
sections.plainLanguage: Success means meeting the original goals and gaining wide use. Wild success means that use grows beyond the original purpose or scale.

sections.title: Factors That Support Initial Adoption
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven initial success factors: positive value from meeting a real need, incremental deployability, open code, freedom from usage restrictions, open specifications, open maintenance, and sound technical design. The case studies suggest that meeting a real need and allowing early adopters to benefit without universal coordination are especially important.

The costs of deployment include hardware changes, operational disruption, retraining, and changes to business arrangements. A protocol has a stronger adoption case when organizations that pay these costs also receive the benefits.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol is easier to adopt when it solves a real problem and early users can benefit without waiting for everyone else. Deployment cost and who receives the benefit also matter.

sections.title: Factors Behind Wider Success
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three factors that help a protocol grow beyond its original use: extensibility, no hard scalability limit near the intended scale, and adequate mitigation of threats. These factors may not determine initial adoption, but they can affect whether a protocol handles new uses and larger deployment.

The case studies compare HTTP and earlier information services, IPv4 and IPX, SSH, inter-domain multicast, WAP, WEP, RADIUS and TACACS+, and NAT. The examples show that design quality alone did not decide initial success; ease of adoption and available value also mattered.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol that becomes widely used needs room to grow and must handle increased scale and security threats. The RFC's examples show that technical quality alone does not determine early adoption.

sections.title: Questions for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
The RFC recommends asking whether a protocol fills a real need, whether implementers and customers are ready, and whether deployment complexity can be reduced. It also asks whether the protocol can work beneath existing applications and whether it can be extended to address future shortcomings.

When success is uncertain, the RFC raises whether the market should choose among alternatives before standardization or whether the IETF should develop multiple options. It advises evaluating initial success factors early and considering wider-success factors when revising an already successful protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol designers should assess need, deployment cost, and who is ready to implement and use the design. A successful protocol may later need changes to handle growth or new uses.
